column6: The commentary supplies an unnamed rain between 87:4's pasture and 87:5's residue; this verse says God covers heaven with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow on hills, giving that whole vertical sequence in one scene.
The commentary says God brings pasture out without naming water; Job describes rain reaching desolate land and causing tender grass to sprout, specifying the same life-giving result.
The commentary traces a line from the Most High through rain to pasture; Isaiah says rain descends from heaven, waters earth, and makes it sprout, then compares that efficacy to God's word.

The commentary reconstructs rain as the missing cause of pasture; Zechariah joins a request for seasonal rain to storm clouds, showers, and plants in the field, making the same weather-to-growth link explicit.

The commentary closes by recalling Moses and links divine guidance with pasture; Moses' song pictures teaching as rain and words as dew falling on grass, joining revelation to the scene's weather and growth.

The commentary treats rain as the unnamed link between pasture emerging and its later decay; Rashi reads Genesis' pre-rain plants as waiting for Adam to pray, after which rain falls and vegetation grows.

The commentary glosses 87:1's اسم as “name”; the Hebrew cognate שֵׁם appears in a call to praise God's name, which the verse says is exalted above earth and heaven, closely joining name-praise with height.

The commentary describes 87:4 as God concretely bringing pasture out; Genesis has God command the earth to bring forth vegetation and seed-bearing plants, adding the creation scene in which the ground yields plant life.

The commentary says المرعى carries grass, grazing, and pasture-place together; this verse says God makes grass grow for cattle and plants for human use, setting pasture in its provision-for-creatures context.

The commentary contrasts the pasture's decay with a source-labeled plant family whose plants do not dry in summer; Jeremiah's water-fed tree has green leaves and does not stop bearing fruit when heat comes.

The commentary explains غثاء as dried vegetation gathered and carried off by a flood; Psalm 1 likens the wicked to chaff driven away by wind, applying field residue to human moral fate while changing the force that carries it.
The commentary follows pasture from green life to dry debris; Isaiah says grass withers and the field flower fades, then uses that plant cycle to describe mortal human glory.

The commentary calls rain life for earth and later treats the plant's life and death alongside the hereafter; Hosea promises Israel revival and likens the Lord's coming to seasonal rains that water the land, joining renewal to rain.

The commentary sets pasture that dries against source-labeled plants said not to dry in summer; Psalm 1's person rooted beside streams remains fruitful with an unwithered leaf, an ethical image of sustained greenness.

The commentary contrasts the pasture's short life with plants said not to dry in summer; this verse says the righteous still bear fruit in old age and remain green, extending that counter-image into a portrait of enduring life.

The commentary notes that Qur'anic غثاء can describe people swept away after a cry; Wisdom has the wicked confess that their life and hope vanish like wind-driven chaff, carrying the plant-debris image into judgment.

The commentary traces plant life into dry residue and then places a person in fire; Hebrews says thorn-bearing land is rejected and ends in burning, joining failed growth and fire in an ethical warning.

column5: farmer awaits early and late rain
column6: The commentary reconstructs rain as what brings pasture from earth and notes the first rain's seasonal mark; James tells farmers to wait patiently for precious fruit through the early and late rains, adding the human labor and timing of the crop cycle.

The commentary moves from dead soil through living grass to decay and also discusses life and death; Paul uses a seed that must die before it comes to life to explain resurrection, making the plant cycle an explicit model for bodily renewal.

The commentary says the plant's journey includes both life and death; Jesus compares his own death and resulting many lives to a grain falling into earth and dying, giving the botanical sequence a distinct christological reading.

The commentary explains غثاء as dried plant matter swept together and also describes the person in fire; John the Baptist's image separates grain from chaff and burns the chaff in unquenchable fire, bringing crop residue into judgment.
The commentary's grass dries after greenness and its next image concerns fire; Jesus says branches outside the vine wither, are gathered, and are burned, linking plant desiccation to judgment.

column5: lake of fire called second death
column6: The commentary stresses that the one in the fire neither dies nor lives; Revelation names the lake of fire “the second death,” a direct difference in how the fiery afterlife is framed.

column5: Isaiah's enduring word applied to the gospel
column6: The commentary joins 87:5's fading plant to 87:17's more-lasting hereafter; Peter follows the grass image with the word that endures and identifies it with the proclaimed good news, giving Isaiah's contrast a Christian interpretive application.

The commentary connects the plant's life, death, and reappearance from earth with resurrection; Clement reads a seed buried and decaying in soil as evidence of resurrection, making the botanical sequence an explicit Christian proof-image.

The commentary stresses that rain is absent from 87:4 even as it supplies the missing link; Genesis says shrubs had not yet appeared because there was no rain and no person to work the ground, making the absent conditions explicit.

The commentary reconstructs rain behind pasture emerging but notes that 87:4 does not name it; the next Genesis verse instead has water rise from earth and water its surface, offering a distinct mechanism for the ground's fertility.

The commentary's pasture is a plant-life scene; this royal prayer compares the king's life-giving justice to rain on mown grass and showers on earth, adding a political use for the same agricultural image.

The commentary identifies the first year's rain as the wasmi because it marks earth with growth; Joel's restoration oracle promises former and latter rains, placing seasonal rainfall within a renewed agricultural cycle.

The commentary describes the cloud's first appearance before rain brings life; Elijah's servant sees a small cloud rising from the sea as the first sign of rain after drought, a concrete cloud-to-rain scene.

The commentary links a persistent cloud and wind with the rain that brings pasture; this verse describes the sky darkening with cloud and wind before heavy rain, presenting the same weather sequence in Elijah's drought story.

The commentary labels the Arabic root ر ع ي for المرعى and says the word spans grazing, grass, and place; Ezekiel uses the cognate Hebrew shepherding verb while describing a flock fed in good pasture, grounding the lexical link in a pastoral scene.

The commentary labels يَحْيَىٰ with Arabic root ح ي ي and calls rain ḥayā because it gives earth life; Ezekiel uses cognate Hebrew חיה when God promises life to dry bones, shifting the shared life verb from vegetation to bodily restoration.
The commentary's plant begins in barren earth and receives life through rain; Job says a cut tree can bud again at the scent of water, adding a specific image of renewed growth after apparent loss.

The commentary connects the pasture's brief cycle to 87:17's claim that the hereafter is more lasting; following Isaiah's grass-withers image in the preceding verse, this verse names God's word as what stands forever, a distinct enduring counterpart.

The commentary links 87:7's hiddenness to weak lightning at cloud edges; Job asks whether a human knows how God commands the clouds and flashes lightning, joining storm signs to limits on human knowledge.

The commentary treats rain as the source of earthly life and links plant life and death to resurrection imagery; the Talmud places the divine keys of rain and resurrection together, making their shared dependence on God's power explicit without equating them.

The commentary follows rain-fed pasture from emergence toward decay; Hebrews describes land drinking repeated rain and yielding a useful crop, using the agricultural response as a moral image of what a received gift produces.

The commentary compresses a plant's entire life into emergence and dry residue; Mark's seed grows through blade, head, and ripe grain before harvest, expanding the same field process into successive stages.

column5: living grass thrown into an oven
column6: The commentary distinguishes the plant's ordinary green-to-dry cycle from the person who neither lives nor dies in fire; Jesus says field grass is alive today and tomorrow goes into the oven, sharpening that contrast.
The commentary makes pasture's drying a figure for life's short course; James describes scorching heat withering grass and its flower, then compares that loss to a rich person's fading life.

The commentary contrasts the plant's brief worldly cycle with what is more lasting in 87:17; Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal, supplying a Christian formulation of that temporal divide.

The commentary describes a person remaining in fire without death or life; Revelation portrays the condemned as having no rest day or night, a related image of unending suffering with a different emphasis.

The commentary follows pasture from green growth to dry residue; Peter quotes the grass-and-flower image to describe human glory as perishable, carrying the plant's short life into a Christian account of mortality.

The commentary compresses a plant's life into a brief cycle and explains غثاء as vegetation gathered and carried by a flood; Moses' psalm says human life is swept away like a flood and compares people to grass, joining mortality to both images.

The commentary follows pasture from emergence to dry residue; in a psalm attributed to Moses, grass flourishes in the morning and withers by evening, giving the same fast plant cycle a human-mortality setting.

The commentary relates the plant's life and death to 87:13's person who neither dies nor lives, and recalls Moses at the surah's close; Moses' song says God kills and makes alive, making divine control of those states explicit.
The commentary traces grass from green growth to dry residue; this verse says wind passes over the field flower and its place is gone, applying plant disappearance directly to mortal life.

The commentary describes grass emerging in patches and later drying into debris; this curse pictures grass on a roof withering before it can be harvested, adding failed growth rather than a full crop cycle.

column5: water and spirit poured on dry ground
column6: The commentary calls rain the source of earthly life and supplies it as the unstated cause of pasture; Isaiah joins water poured on thirsty ground to God's spirit poured on descendants, giving the rain-and-life image a restoration meaning.
The commentary describes pasture emerging from earth; Isaiah says restored descendants spring up like grass and willows by streams, extending plant growth into a picture of a people renewed.
The commentary links rain to the life of earth and pasture; Hosea says God will be like dew to Israel, which will blossom like a lily, using moisture-fed growth to portray national restoration.

The commentary contrasts the pasture's decay with what lasts; Ezekiel's restored-land vision has trees beside a river whose fruit continues and whose leaves heal, a sustained botanical image in an eschatological setting.

The commentary ends with the hereafter as better and more lasting; Revelation's final vision has a river of life flowing from God's throne, placing life-giving water in the renewed world beyond the plant cycle.

column5: tree of life bears fruit continually
column6: The commentary contrasts the pasture's decay with the hereafter's permanence; Revelation's final city has a tree of life bearing fruit each month with healing leaves, an enduring counter-image to seasonal loss.
The commentary renders 87:1's الأعلى as “Most High”; Genesis uses the cognate Semitic title El Elyon for the creator of heaven and earth, anchoring the shared elevation term in a blessing of God.

The commentary uses rain reviving dead ground as an image for the dead being brought out; Ezekiel says God will open graves and bring Israel up, adding a prophetic restoration scene whose own context identifies the bones with the exiled people.

The commentary sets plant death and life beside the person who neither dies nor lives and the lasting hereafter; Daniel describes sleepers in the dust awakening to everlasting life or disgrace, making final destinies explicit.

column5: breath withdrawn, creatures return to dust
column6: The commentary describes vegetation's passage between life and death; this verse says creatures die and return to dust when God withdraws their breath, framing death as the withdrawal of life-giving power.

The commentary says the Creator brings pasture out and links rain-fed growth with life; this verse says God sends his spirit, creates living things, and renews the face of the ground, joining creaturely life to renewed earth.

column5: God gives each seed its body
column6: The commentary says God brings pasture out of earth and compares the plant's life and death with resurrection; Paul says God gives each seed its own body, connecting divine creation to the form that emerges from sowing.

The commentary moves from plant decay to 87:17's more-lasting hereafter; Paul describes the resurrection body as sown perishable and raised imperishable, making permanence the direct outcome of the death-and-growth analogy.

The commentary connects the plant's cycle to what is more lasting; Peter says believers are born again from imperishable seed through God's living word, adding regeneration as the durable counterpart to perishable growth.

column5: sowing reaps corruption or eternal life
column6: The commentary contrasts the pasture's short worldly life with the better, more lasting hereafter; Paul says sowing to flesh reaps corruption while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life, turning field work into an ethical choice of destinies.

The commentary says المرعى includes grass, grazing, and the place of grazing; the psalm's shepherd leads a speaker to green pastures and still waters, giving the term a concrete setting of rest and nourishment.

The commentary joins the plant's disappearance to the claim that the hereafter lasts; after the preceding grass-and-wind image, this verse says God's steadfast love lasts from everlasting to everlasting, supplying a different enduring counterpart.

The commentary says first growth appears unevenly, in some places but not others; this verse describes God watering furrows, softening clods with showers, and blessing growth, adding the prepared-soil detail behind that patchy emergence.

The commentary traces a vertical movement from the Most High through rain to pasture; Isaiah calls for the heavens to pour down and the earth to open so salvation and righteousness sprout, giving the plant image a moral-restoration sense.

The commentary connects the Most High with clouds that nurture plants; this theophany surrounds God with clouds and thick darkness while grounding his throne in justice, making cloud a sign of divine presence as well as weather.

The commentary describes weak lightning at cloud edges and says God knows what is hidden; this verse says God's lightning lights the world and the earth sees and trembles, pairing a visible storm sign with divine sovereignty.

The commentary says the south wind sustains a cloud and links its Arabic root family to 87:11; Job describes the south wind making garments hot, adding a distinct weather effect for the same named wind.

column5: cloud guides Israel, fire lights night
column6: The commentary develops cloud, weak lightning, and a Moses connection; Exodus says God leads Israel by a cloud in daytime and fire at night, adding a guidance scene where cloud and light mark the divine route.

column5: cloud as covering, fire by night
column6: The commentary explains the sky as what rises over and shades, then describes night lightning around clouds; this Exodus retelling says God spread a cloud as covering and gave fire for night light, joining shade and illumination in one image.

The commentary notes that المرعى names grass, the place, and grazing; Jesus says those who enter through him will be saved and find pasture, giving the pastoral word a Christian image of access and nourishment.

The commentary treats 87:1's رب as “Lord” and develops its Arabic family separately; John records the Semitic address Rabbi and explains it as teacher, showing a cognate title in an interpersonal teaching context.
